exercises.name: Seated Climb
instructions: Add resistance or pick a gear that slows your cadence but still lets the pedals turn smoothly.
Stay in the saddle with the hands relaxed on the bars and the elbows slightly bent.
Keep the upper body still and the head up while the legs drive an even, round pedal stroke.
Hold a steady cadence, shifting to an easier gear before it turns into a grind.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rocking the upper body and gripping the bars hard, or grinding a gear that is too big.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use less resistance and keep each climb to 2 or 3 minutes.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Seated climbing is the efficient way to hold power for long efforts.

exercises.name: Standing Climb
instructions: Add a gear or a little resistance just before you leave the saddle.
Rise smoothly and keep the hips back over the saddle rather than far forward over the bars.
Let the bike move slightly under you while the pedal stroke stays smooth.
Sit back down, ease the resistance and return to a steady seated cadence.
exercises.commonMistakes: Standing in a gear that is too light so the legs spin out, or throwing the body weight over the front wheel.
exercises.beginnerModification: Stand for 10 to 15 seconds at a time with moderate resistance.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Standing gives a short burst of extra force for steep sections and a break for the seated muscles.

exercises.name: Low-Cadence Climb
instructions: Warm up for at least 10 minutes at an easy spin.
Choose a resistance that drops your cadence about 10 rpm below your normal climbing rhythm.
Stay seated and push through the whole pedal circle for about 8 minutes with steady breathing.
Spin easily for several minutes and repeat up to three times.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rocking the hips and pulling on the bars to force the gear over, or doing it without a proper warm-up.
exercises.beginnerModification: Shorten each effort to 3 or 4 minutes and drop the cadence only slightly.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Pushing a bigger gear builds the leg strength that makes normal climbing gears feel lighter.

exercises.name: Spin-Ups
instructions: Set a light resistance and pedal at a comfortable cadence.
Over about 30 seconds, raise the cadence steadily until it is as fast as you can hold without bouncing.
Hold that leg speed briefly with the hips still on the saddle.
Let the cadence come back down and spin easily for 1 to 2 minutes before the next one.
exercises.commonMistakes: Bouncing on the saddle, or adding resistance so it becomes a strength effort.
exercises.beginnerModification: Stop the build as soon as the hips start to bounce and hold just below that cadence.
exercises.whyThisMatters: High leg speed at low load smooths the pedal stroke and coordination.

exercises.name: Cadence Change Drill
instructions: Sit with the sit bones on the widest part of the saddle and set a moderate resistance.
Pedal for 1 minute at 80 rpm, 1 minute at 90 rpm and 1 minute at 100 rpm.
Change the order of the three cadences on the next block without changing resistance.
Spin easily for 60 seconds between blocks.
exercises.commonMistakes: Stamping on the downstroke only, or easing the resistance right off to hit the faster cadences.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use two cadences, 80 and 90 rpm, and a lighter resistance.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Switching leg speed on demand teaches control of the pedal stroke across the range.

exercises.name: Sweet-Spot Interval
instructions: Warm up for 10 to 15 minutes, building gradually from easy to moderate.
Settle at an effort just below threshold, hard but steady, with breathing deep and controlled.
Hold that effort and a steady cadence for the full interval, building toward 20 minutes.
Spin easily for 5 minutes, repeat once, then cool down.
exercises.formCue: Hard, but you could go longer.
exercises.commonMistakes: Starting above the target and fading, or letting the effort drift down to an easy ride.
exercises.beginnerModification: Ride intervals of 8 to 10 minutes and add time over several weeks.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Long efforts just under threshold give a lot of aerobic training for a manageable recovery cost.

exercises.name: Bike Sprint Interval
instructions: Warm up thoroughly, including two or three short hard efforts.
From a steady roll, add resistance and sprint at full effort for 15 to 30 seconds with cadence above 90 rpm.
Keep the upper body firm and the pedal stroke as smooth as you can at speed.
Spin very easily until you are ready to match the quality of the first sprint, then go again.
exercises.commonMistakes: Cutting the recovery so the sprints become medium efforts, or sprinting cold.
exercises.beginnerModification: Sprint seated for 10 seconds with long, easy recoveries.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Short all-out efforts build top-end power and the ability to repeat it.

exercises.name: Arms-and-Body Rowing Drill
instructions: Sit tall at the finish position with the legs straight and the handle drawn in below the ribs.
Keeping the legs flat, extend the arms first and then swing the body forward from the hips.
Swing the body back and then draw the arms in, in that order.
Row this way for a minute or two, then add the legs and row full strokes with the same sequence.
exercises.commonMistakes: Bending the knees before the hands have passed them, or pulling with the arms before the body swings.
exercises.beginnerModification: Start with arms only, then add the body swing once that is smooth.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Isolating the upper half of the stroke fixes the order of movement on the recovery.

exercises.name: Legs-Only Rowing Drill
instructions: Sit at the catch with shins near vertical, arms straight and the body leaning forward from the hips.
Push with the legs while the arms stay straight and the body keeps its forward angle.
Stop when the legs are almost flat, without leaning back or bending the arms.
Slide forward under control and repeat, then build back to full strokes.
exercises.commonMistakes: Letting the seat shoot back ahead of the handle, or opening the back early.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use a low damper setting and move slowly through each push.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It teaches the legs to start the drive, which is where most of the stroke's power comes from.

exercises.name: Rowing Pause Drill
instructions: Row full strokes at a low stroke rate.
On each recovery, stop for a second once the arms are straight and the body has swung forward, before the knees bend.
Check that the hands are past the knees, then slide forward to the catch and take the next stroke.
After a few minutes, remove the pause and keep the same order of movement.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rushing through the pause, or sliding forward before the hands have cleared the knees.
exercises.beginnerModification: Pause on every second or third stroke instead of every stroke.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A deliberate stop makes you feel the correct sequence before blending it into one motion.

exercises.name: Rowing Rhythm Count
instructions: Row at a low stroke rate with light to moderate pressure.
Count one as you drive back quickly with the legs, body and arms.
Count two, three and four as you move forward slowly through the recovery.
Keep the count going so the drive stays quick and the recovery stays unhurried.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rushing forward on the slide so the drive and recovery take the same time.
exercises.beginnerModification: Say the count out loud and row with very light pressure.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A slower recovery gives a moment of rest every stroke, which is what makes long rows sustainable.

exercises.name: Rowing Steady State
exercises.musclesWorked: Quads, glutes, lats, upper back, core
instructions: Warm up with 5 minutes of easy rowing.
Settle at a stroke rate in the mid 20s and an effort you could hold a conversation through.
Keep the same split and rate for the whole piece, with legs, then body, then arms on each drive.
Finish with a few minutes of light rowing.
exercises.commonMistakes: Letting the stroke rate climb as you tire while each stroke gets shorter and weaker.
exercises.beginnerModification: Break the session into 5-minute blocks with a minute of easy paddling between them.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Long, even rowing builds aerobic fitness and gives hundreds of strokes of technique practice.

exercises.name: Rowing Rate Ladder
exercises.musclesWorked: Quads, glutes, lats, upper back, core
instructions: Warm up, then start rowing at a low stroke rate with firm pressure.
After a set time, such as 2 to 3 minutes, raise the rate by two strokes per minute.
Keep stepping the rate up at each change while holding the same stroke length and sequence.
Come back down the same steps, then row lightly to cool down.
exercises.commonMistakes: Shortening the stroke to hit the higher rates, or speeding up the slide instead of the drive.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use only three steps and keep the top rate within a comfortable range.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Changing rate on command teaches you to hold good strokes as the tempo rises.

exercises.name: Negative-Split Row
exercises.musclesWorked: Quads, glutes, lats, upper back, core
instructions: Row easily for a few minutes and note the 500-metre split you can hold comfortably.
Divide the piece into equal blocks and row the first block at that comfortable split.
Make each following block slightly faster, pushing harder with the legs rather than rushing the slide.
Row the last block at a strong effort, then paddle lightly to recover.
exercises.commonMistakes: Going out too fast so later blocks slow down, or raising the stroke rate without adding leg drive.
exercises.beginnerModification: Use only two blocks, the second a little quicker than the first.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Building pace through a piece teaches pacing control and a strong finish.

exercises.name: Freestyle Catch-Up Drill
instructions: Push off and swim freestyle with a steady kick.
Leave the leading arm stretched out in front of its shoulder while the other arm takes a full stroke.
Bring the recovering hand forward to meet the leading hand before the next arm starts its pull.
Keep the hands in line with the shoulders rather than crossing the centre line.
exercises.formCue: One arm waits for the other.
exercises.commonMistakes: Letting the hands cross in front of the head, or letting the kick stop while the arm waits.
exercises.beginnerModification: Hold a kickboard out front and swap hands on the board with each stroke.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Slowing the stroke down fixes hand entry and timing at the front of the stroke.

exercises.name: One-Arm Freestyle Drill
instructions: Push off with one arm resting by the side and the other ready to stroke.
Swim freestyle with the working arm only, keeping a steady kick.
Breathe on every stroke toward the side of the resting arm.
Rotate the body to both sides, then switch arms on the next length.
exercises.formCue: Rotate both ways, even with one arm.
exercises.commonMistakes: Swimming flat with no body rotation, or lifting the head forward to breathe.
exercises.beginnerModification: Wear fins so the kick holds the body position while you learn the rotation.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It exposes a flat body position and trains rotation and breath timing.

exercises.name: Swim Kick Set
exercises.musclesWorked: Hip flexors, glutes, quads, hamstrings, core
instructions: Push off in a long line on the front, side or back with the arms still.
Kick from the hips with a small, quick flutter, letting the knees and ankles stay loose.
Point the toes backward and keep the kick narrow.
Kick one length, rest briefly and repeat, changing between side, front and back.
exercises.commonMistakes: Kicking from the knees with big bends, or arching the back to hold the head up on a board.
exercises.beginnerModification: Kick on the back with fins so breathing is easy and the body stays level.
exercises.whyThisMatters: A narrow hip-driven kick holds the body level, which makes every stroke easier.

exercises.name: Pull Buoy Set
instructions: Place a pull buoy between the thighs and push off with the legs still.
After each hand enters, let the hand drop down and in while the elbow bends and points out to the side.
Press straight back against the water, speeding the hand up through the pull.
Finish just past the hip and bring the arm forward relaxed.
exercises.commonMistakes: Pressing down on the water with a straight arm, or dropping the elbow at the start of the pull.
exercises.beginnerModification: Swim short repeats of one length with plenty of rest and an easy stroke rate.
exercises.whyThisMatters: With the legs supported, all attention can go to how the arms hold and move water.

exercises.name: Freestyle Breathing Drill
instructions: Stand in shallow water and practise bobs, breathing out steadily underwater and in quickly at the surface.
Push off and swim easy freestyle, breathing out through the nose and mouth the whole time the face is down.
To breathe, turn the head with the body's rotation and keep one goggle in the water.
Take a quick breath, return the face to the water and carry on the stroke without a pause.
exercises.formCue: Breathe out under, turn to breathe in.
exercises.commonMistakes: Lifting the head forward, which sinks the hips, or holding the breath underwater.
exercises.beginnerModification: Kick on the side with the bottom arm extended and practise turning the face in and out of the water.
exercises.whyThisMatters: Calm, low breathing keeps the body level and lets you swim further for less effort.

exercises.name: Backstroke
exercises.musclesWorked: Lats, shoulders, triceps, core, hip flexors
instructions: Lie on the back near the surface with the head still, ears in the water and hips high.
Kick from the hips with the legs close together, ankles loose and knees only slightly bent.
Lift one arm out thumb first, keep it straight overhead and enter the water little finger first.
Catch the water, push through to the thigh and breathe in a steady rhythm with the arm cycle.
exercises.commonMistakes: Carrying the head too high so the hips sink, or pulling hard the instant the hand enters.
exercises.beginnerModification: Kick on the back with arms by the sides, then add one arm at a time.
exercises.whyThisMatters: It works the back of the shoulders and lets you breathe freely, which balances a lot of freestyle.

exercises.name: Breaststroke
instructions: Start in a long glide, face down, with the body close to level and arms extended.
Sweep the hands out and down with the elbows high, then in toward the chest as the shoulders rise and you breathe in.
Draw the heels toward the seat, turn the feet out and kick round and back until the legs come together.
Reach the arms forward and glide in a straight line, breathing out, before the next stroke.
exercises.commonMistakes: Pulling the hands too wide and too far back, or kicking while the arms are still pulling.
exercises.beginnerModification: Practise the kick on its own with a board, then add one pull to every two kicks.
exercises.whyThisMatters: The glide makes it a sustainable stroke, and the legs do most of the work.
